title: Bellarmine prefers the middle way: no perpetual doubt, yet not faith-certainty of pardon
source_text: XXII. Huic sententiae accedit Bellarminus, lib. 3. de Justif. cap. 11. Responsione ad postremam rationem. Ubi postquam asseruit nullum esse Catholicum scriptorem, qui doceat oportere homines perpetuo dubitare, & haesitare de sua cum Deo reconciliatione, tres refert Catholicorum suorum sententias. Primam Catharini, qui justis tribuit certitudinem fidei divinae de sua justificatione: secundam, eorum qui putant posse justos ad eam securitatem venire, ut nullam habeant de sua justificatione formidinem: & tertiam, quam ipse probat, ut veriorem & communiorem, quae non tollit quidem omnem formidinem, tamen tollit omnem anxietatem & haesitationem, & ipsam etiam dubitationem, si dubius dicatur qui non audet alteri parti assentiri. Neque enim, inquit, bona est argumentatio, Catholici non habent certitudinem fidei de sua justificatione, igitur semper dubitant, haerent, anxii sunt; sicut neque contra quis recte concluderet: Catholici non sunt anxii, neque haesitant de sua justificatione, igitur certi sunt certitudine fidei sibi remissa esse peccata. Datur enim aliquid medium inter haec extrema, videlicet, certitudo quaedam moralis ex parte intellectus, & spes, ac fiducia, ex parte voluntatis. Quibus consona sunt quae scribit ejusdem libri cap. 3. §. Deinde. Neque enim, inquit, Catholici negant, certam fiduciam in Deo collocandam esse, & certo confidendum post actam legitime poenitentiam, & Sacramentum Baptismi, vel Absolutionis rite perceptum, remissa esse peccata. Sed adversarii, ut fidem cum fiducia, ita certitudinem fidei cum certitudine fiduciae confundunt. Cap. vero decimo, §. Vides igitur, concedit ex poenitentiae fructibus, ut ex signis quibusdam, gigni persuasionem & securitatem gratiae, non tamen certitudinem fidei Catholicae, vel Divinae.
pass_a_gloss: Bellarmine accedes to this opinion in On Justification, book 3, chapter 11, in the Reply to the last reason. Where after he has asserted that there is no Catholic writer who teaches that people ought perpetually to doubt and hesitate concerning their reconciliation with God, he reports three opinions of his Catholics. The first of Catharinus, who attributes to the just the certainty of divine faith concerning their justification; the second, of those who think the just can come to such security that they have no fear concerning their justification; and the third, which he himself approves as truer and more common, which does not indeed take away every fear, yet takes away every anxiety and hesitation, and even doubt itself, if he is called doubtful who does not dare assent to either side. For, he says, the argumentation is not good: Catholics do not have the certainty of faith concerning their justification, therefore they always doubt, stick, and are anxious; just as neither would anyone rightly conclude the contrary: Catholics are not anxious, nor do they hesitate concerning their justification, therefore they are certain with the certainty of faith that their sins have been remitted to them. For something middle is given between these extremes, namely a certain moral certainty on the side of the intellect, and hope and trust on the side of the will. Things agreeable to this are what he writes in chapter 3 of the same book, section ‘Then.’ For neither, he says, do Catholics deny that certain trust is to be placed in God, and that after penance lawfully performed and the sacrament of baptism or of absolution duly received one ought certainly to trust that sins have been remitted. But the adversaries, as they confuse faith with trust, so confuse the certainty of faith with the certainty of trust. And in chapter 10, section ‘You see therefore,’ he grants that from the fruits of repentance, as from certain signs, a persuasion and security of grace is begotten, yet not the certainty of Catholic or divine faith.
pass_b_english: Bellarmine rejects both Catharinus’s faith-certainty and fearless moral security.
His middle way clears anxious doubt while still denying divine-faith certainty; penitential signs yield persuasion, not Catholic faith-certainty.
